name: set-ops
axis: hash set: build two overlapping string sets, then intersection / difference by membership test
n: n=100000 elements per set, overlap n/2, r=100 passes of 2n membership tests (20M `has` calls: 10M hit, 10M miss), 1 values() iteration
nPython: n=25000, r=100 (4x smaller sets and 4x fewer tests; scales linearly in n)
notes: VL's Set surface is `.add`/`.has`/`.delete`/`.length`/`.values()` and NOTHING else — there is no set ALGEBRA. Rust has `a.intersection(&b)`, Python has `a & b` / `a - b`, and V8 14.9 has the ES2025 `a.intersection(b)`; VL has none, so the explicit membership loop is the only VL spelling and is therefore what all four run (same algorithm, rule 1). If the built-in operators had been used instead, Python and Rust would have been measuring C/library set algebra against a VL interpreter loop. The membership loops walk the backing ARRAYS rather than iterating the sets, so the measurement is `has`, not iteration. B's elements are built in their own loop so an element of A-intersect-B is a different string object in B than in A (see ../map-string/meta.json on the `ref.eq` shortcut). Verified separately: VL's `Set.has` and `Map[k]` cost the same (610ms vs 611ms for 10M probes of a 100k table), so there is no Set-specific overhead in VL.
